To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the metabolic cost of walking up a gradient is higher than on level ground, (2) walking up a gradient increases the duty factor and stance time, and (3) the metabolic cost is not lower when descending a gradient.
the metabolic cost of walking uphill is greater than on level ground at similar speeds, but that the metabolic cost is not reduced when walking downhill.
the energy cost of walking uphill is higher than walking level and the energy cost of level walking is higher than walking downhill, and that walking uphill requires a waddling (increased duty) gait.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolic cost of walking and the associated kinematics on a gradient.
the metabolic cost of locomotion on gradients and, in particular, the effects of a waddling (as opposed to bipedal) gait.
understanding how the metabolic cost of walking is affected by the gradient of the surface.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cost of walking on slopes varies between species, and is dependent upon the interaction of a number of variables.
there are no general rules governing the metabolic cost of locomotion on gradients.
there is not a single metabolic cost of walking up or down a gradient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metabolic cost of locomotion on gradients is not only a function of speed and gradient, but is also affected by gait.
, in general, walking uphill is more metabolically expensive than walking downhill, but that this is not always the case.

, for the barnacle goose, the metabolic cost of walking uphill is increased due to the increased duty factor, and walking downhill is increased due to a choppy stride and perhaps a reduced ability to adopt a more efficient posture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic cost of walking uphill is not simply a consequence of increased mechanical work done to move uphill.
the metabolic cost of walking is not a constant across gradients, and that the cost of locomotion on slopes is not simply determined by the mechanical work required to overcome gravity.
the metabolic costs of walking on gradients are highly dependent on an organism's posture and the way in which they generate locomotor force.
